newsitem.title: GERMANY: BT-MCI merger could spark global shake-up.
newsitem.headline: BT-MCI merger could spark global shake-up.

text.p: A major realignment of the world's telecommunications industry could be imminent as regional alliances assess their positions after the merger of British Telecommunications Plc and MCI Communications, industry analysts said on Monday.

But should the BT-MCI merger be concluded as planned, their newly formed Concert Plc could breakthrough as the industry leader that the world's largest corporations and regional carriers with global aspirations turn to for services.

Because the global marketplace is increasingly dependent on offering a broad range of services across all types of networks from fixed wire to mobile and satellite services, only large, global enterprises are expected to survive.
Through the merger, BT and MCI would come closest to achieving true global player status with Concert.

"In order to be a successful global company, you have to be successful in two of the top three world markets," said George Verghese, London-based analyst with Commerzbank. "Given that they (BT and MCI) have critical mass in both America and Europe, they now have the basis to build a global business."

Following the BT-MCI announcement, speculation emerged that France Telecom and Deutsche Telekom might want to raise their stake in Sprint Corp. That speculation initially fuelled a rise in the U.S. carrier's shares.

But analysts said it was unlikely their Global One venture or the WorldPartners network alliance of global giant AT&T Corp that includes Kokusai Denshin Denwa of Japan could consolidate their international assets anytime soon to rival Concert.
"There are too many political obstacles," said Mike Grant of Analysys Ltd, the telecoms consultancy based in Cambridge, England.

The French and German carriers would likely face a groundswell of opposition to any effort to acquire Sprint because of what is perceived in the United States as a slow move by those countries to deregulate their home markets.
Thus, the arguement is further enhanced for Concert to emerge as the telecommunications leader.
Despite Concert's lead, however, some analysts noted Global One could be making up loss ground.

"Global One's products are somewhat less sophisticated than those available from Concert but otherwise, broadly match the offerings available from rival alliances," wrote analysts for ABN Amro Hoare Govett in a recent report on Deutsche Telekom.
Meanwhile, another rival alliance, Unisource, formed in 1991 between equal owners Swiss PTT, Telia of Sweden, the Dutch KPN group and Telefonica of Spain, has links to AT&T.
However, there has been ongoing speculation that Unisource has run into trouble because of difficulties in managing what has become an unwieldy alliance.

The involvement of Spain's Telefonica has added regulatory difficulties because the European Commission is unhappy with Spain's efforts to open its telecoms market. The venture's chief executive also recently switched to rival Global One.
But analysts did not think Unisource would break up. There is too much at stake for its members.
"One possibilty is that it moves en bloc to Global One or even Cable and Wireless," said Grant. "And Cable and Wireless might now be interested in getting together with AT&T to counter BT-MCI."
But BT-MCI's Concert is expected to gain strategic and important financial advantages by cutting the cost of carrying traffic between the United States and Europe.
That type of solid base, coupled with earlier benefits gained when BT and MCI first formed an alliance in 1993, was seen eventually attracting potential Asian partners.

BT and MCI's alliance in 1993 was one of the first of a series of telecoms partnerships to provide "seamless" services, which are a broad array of communications services that are the same regardless of where a company has its office and offer global billing, customer management and support.

Typical seamless services include fast data transmission, satellite services and managed bandwidth, which saves a company money by allowing it to buy transmission capacity for specified periods of time.
